questions.q: In the vectorized backtester example, what does `.fillna(0)` on the strategy returns accomplish?
options: It removes look-ahead bias entirely
It prevents NaN values from the rolling-window warm-up period from corrupting the compounded equity curve
It guarantees the strategy is profitable
It converts the signal from integer to boolean
questions.explain: Before the rolling windows have enough data, computations produce NaN. Filling those with 0 ensures the cumulative product used for the equity curve isn't poisoned by NaN propagation.

questions.q: In the event-driven backtester, the decision at step i uses `prev` (the bar before today) and fills at `today['open']`. Why fill at the open rather than at the price that generated the signal?
options: Because the open price is always higher
Because the signal is only known after the prior bar closes, so the earliest realistic fill is the next bar's open
Because open prices are easier to download
It's an arbitrary stylistic choice with no real consequence
questions.explain: This mirrors the vectorized .shift(1): a decision based on a completed bar can only be acted on starting the following bar, and the open of that next bar is a reasonable, achievable fill point.

questions.q: Why can a vectorized and event-driven backtest of the 'same' strategy produce slightly different results?
options: One of them must contain a bug
They embed different reasonable assumptions — e.g. continuous fractional positions vs. whole-share sizing, or close-to-close vs. next-open fills
Event-driven backtests always ignore transaction costs
Vectorized backtests cannot process real price data
questions.explain: The differences come from legitimate implementation choices — fill price conventions, position sizing granularity, and warm-up handling — not from one approach being broken.

questions.q: Besides total return, which of these should a backtester report at minimum, per this lesson?
options: Only the strategy's name and author
The equity curve path, CAGR, annualized volatility/Sharpe, trade count, and max drawdown
Only the number of lines of code used
Only the final cash balance
questions.explain: A single total-return number hides how the return was achieved. Reporting the path, risk-adjusted metrics, trade count, and drawdown gives a much more honest picture of the strategy.

questions.q: What is the key takeaway from building both engines for the same strategy?
options: Vectorized backtests should never be trusted
The assumptions embedded in a backtester's code (fills, sizing, warm-up handling) are themselves part of the strategy's measured performance
Event-driven backtests are obsolete now that vectorized tools exist
Both engines will always produce identical results if coded correctly
questions.explain: The lesson's central point is that a strategy's signal rule alone doesn't fully determine the backtest result — the surrounding implementation choices matter and should be made deliberately, not accidentally.
